children: Solar cell and module manufacturer GREW Solar recently announced a five-year commercialisation partnership with US-headquartered Caelux Corporation to produce high-power hybrid-tandem solar modules using Caelux’s ‘energy producing glass’. Here, the glass covering the solar cells itself is an energy producing layer.

Caelux achieves this by coating the glass with a thin film of perovskites. Vish Iyer, Managing Director–India and West Asia, says the perovskite layer captures sunlight that the silicon cell cannot use as efficiently, while the cell itself continues to perform as before.

The solar industry has focused on two approaches to perovskite technology: Integrating perovskite into the silicon solar cell and developing perovskite as an energy producing layer. Caelux’s R&D focused on the latter, Iyer tells businessline.

The distinction is important. In the conventional perovskite-silicon tandem approach, the perovskite is deposited directly on the silicon cell, requiring changes to cell architecture and perhaps new manufacturing equipment. Caelux, instead, deposits the perovskite solar layer on the glass that normally serves as the module’s front cover.
“In effect, we turn that inert glass into an energy producing layer,” Iyer says.
Caelux solar modules with ‘energy producing glass’

This allows the use of existing silicon module factories and equipment. Caelux says its energy producing glass can be paired with mono-PERC, TOPCon, back contact and heterojunction technologies, and with modules 1.7-2.5 m long.
Rather than replacing silicon, it is about adding another generator to the same module.
For instance, a 10 GW TOPCon manufacturing line could, according to Caelux, produce the equivalent of 12 GW of module output after incorporating its technology with limited additional investment.
The higher power density could also reduce the requirement of land, mounting structures, cabling and other components.

Caelux has signed agreements with Indian manufacturers, including Rayzon Solar and Navitas Solar, for 5 GW hybrid-tandem production. Together, with the GREW Solar deal, its contracted volume with module manufacturers globally is 19 GW.
The Indian partnerships target commercial production from 2028. Navitas and Rayzon target 28 per cent efficiency with TOPCon-based modules, while GREW’s modules target efficiencies above 29 per cent.

“Perovskite-silicon tandem could be an important breakthrough for the solar industry, enabling significantly higher power from the same module area,” Vineet Mittal, Director-Finance and Strategy, Navitas Solar, says. “If successfully commercialised at scale, moving module efficiencies from around 23 per cent today towards 28 per cent and beyond could strengthen India’s ability to manufacture next-generation, high-efficiency solar modules for both domestic and international markets.”
Perovskite is a thin-film technology, and the challenge is in depositing a uniform layer over a large area and ensuring it survives decades of outdoor exposure.
Caelux says years of R&D have gone into solving these issues. The company shipped the first commercial order of its active glass technology in 2025.
Its medium-term plan includes production in India, alongside its US operations.
The next generation of solar modules may not require abandoning the old one but simply making the glass work.

title: When solar glass becomes a power generator
